Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 97, verses 1–2:

Surat al-Qadr

Abu Hayyan said: It is Medinan according to the majority opinion, and al-Mawardi related the opposite. al-Wahidi mentioned that it is the first surah to have been revealed in Medina. Al-Jalal (al-Suyuti) said in al-Itqan: There are two opinions concerning it, and the majority hold that it is Meccan. Those who hold that it is Medinan cite what al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim narrated, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was shown the Banu Umayyah upon his pulpit, and this grieved him. So there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, and there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾," the hadith.

And it is as al-Muzani said: it is a munkar (rejected) hadith. End of quotation. Al-Jalal (al-Suyuti) narrated this hadith in ad-Durr al-Manthur from Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Dala'il, also through the narration of Yusuf ibn Sa'd, and he mentioned in it that al-Tirmidhi narrated it and declared it weak, and that al-Khatib narrated something similar from Ibn Abbas, and likewise from Ibn al-Musayyib with the wording: "The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I was shown the Banu Umayyah climbing up my pulpit, and this grieved me.' So there was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾."

Regarding al-Muzani's statement that it is munkar, I have some hesitation. Whatever the case, the aspect of its indication that the surah is Medinan has been questioned, and it has been answered that this may be due to his words in it: "upon his pulpit."

The apparent meaning is that the pulpit existed at the time of the vision, and it was only made in Medina. The number of its verses is six in the Meccan and Syrian (readings), and five in other than these two.

There is a hadith narrated by Muhammad ibn Nasr from Anas, raised (to the Prophet ﷺ): "Indeed it equals a quarter of the Qur'an."

Many of the Shafi'is mentioned that it is recommended to recite it after wudu'. Some of their imams said: three times. The point of its connection with what precedes it is that it serves as a reason for the command to recite the Qur'an mentioned earlier, as if it were said: Recite the Qur'an, for its status is great and its affair is magnificent. al-Khattabi said: The intended reference of the pronoun in His words, "in it": ﴿Indeed, We sent it down﴾ is to His words: ﴿Read﴾, and for this reason it was placed after it. Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi approved of this and said: "This is very original." The apparent meaning is that he intended that the hidden pronoun in "that" refers to "Read"... etc., as you will hear, if Allah the Exalted wills. His intending that it refers to the read thing understood from "Read," so that it would mean its return to the Qur'an, is contrary to the apparent meaning, so do not be heedless.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾. The pronoun, according to the majority, refers to the Qur'an, and Imam (al-Razi) claimed the consensus of the exegetes on this, and it seems he did not count the opinion of those among them who held that it refers to Jibril (peace be upon him) or others, due to its weakness. They said: In referring to it with a pronoun of absence, despite the lack of prior mention, there is an extreme exaltation of it, since it indicates that, because of its lofty status, it is as if present with everyone, so it has the force of something mentioned. Likewise in ascribing its sending down to the "We" of majesty twice and in emphasizing the sentence. al-Zamakhshari pointed out that the sentence conveys the exclusivity of the sending down to Him, glorified is He, on the basis that it is of the type: "I strove in your need," where the implicit agent is placed before the verb. It was objected that what they mentioned applies to the detached pronoun and not to the attached one, as in the subject of "inna" here. Yes, exclusivity is understood from the context of the speech. And it was objected that they did not explicitly stipulate the condition mentioned for magnifying the time of its sending down with His words: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾, because it indicates that its sublimity lies beyond the scope of human knowledge; no one knows it or has knowledge of it except the Knower of the unseen, as this suggests.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 97, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾. This is a general explanation of its status, following His raising the Prophet (ﷺ) to the anticipation of knowing it; for that indicates the promise of its being made known to him. It is reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that every instance in the Qur'an of His saying, "What will make you know (ma adraka)," Allah taught His Prophet (ﷺ) about it, and every instance of His saying, "And what will make you know (wa ma yudrika)," He did not inform him of it.

The manner of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the two sentences has already been explained. In the display of "the Night of Decree" in both places there is an emphasis on its magnitude and grandeur that is not hidden. The meaning of its revelation (inzal) therein is the revelation of the whole of the Qur'an at once, from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to the lowest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya). It is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The Qur'an was revealed on the Night of Decree all at once to the lowest heaven, and it was in the places of the stars (mawaqi' al-nujum). And Allah, exalted is He, would reveal it to His Messenger (ﷺ) part after part." In another narration, instead of "and it was in the places of the stars...," etc. Then it was revealed after that over twenty years. In another narration from him as well: "The Qur'an was revealed all at once until it was placed in the House of Honour (Bayt al-'Izza) in the heaven, and Jibril (peace be upon him) brought it down to Muhammad (ﷺ) in reply to the words and deeds of the servants." In another: that it was revealed in Ramadan, on the Night of Decree, all at once, then it was revealed to the places of the stars as messengers in the months and days. That the revelation afterward took place over twenty years is one opinion; and some said, and this is the most well-known, over twenty-three; and another said over twenty-five. This difference relates to the disagreement over the length of his (ﷺ) stay in Makkah after the Prophethood (al-ba'th).

Al-Sha'bi said: the meaning is "We began its revelation therein." The well-known view is that the first verses revealed were "Read (iqra')," and that its revelation was at Hira' during the day.

Yes, in al-Bahr it is related that the descent of the angel at Hira' was in the last ten nights of Ramadan. If that is authentic and the intended meaning is that it was at night, then well and good; otherwise the apparent sense of al-Sha'bi's statement is not consistent. Unless it is said that he meant the beginning of its revelation to the lowest heaven was therein, and that this need not coincide with the beginning of its revelation to him (ﷺ) in time. Furthermore, in "We revealed it (anzalnahu)," according to what has been mentioned, there is a figurative usage in the attribution, because what belongs to a part is attributed to the whole, or it is a metaphor of the container (majaz al-taraf), or it is an implicit meaning (tadmin). It has also been said: the meaning is the revelation of it from the Tablet to the lowest heaven in installments, on the nights of decree, with "a night" (bi-laylati) being generic. It is said that the Qur'an was revealed to the lowest heaven on twenty nights of decree, or twenty-three, or twenty-five, and on each night was revealed what Allah, exalted is He, decreed for its revelation during that whole year; then He would reveal it, glory be to Him, in portions throughout the year. This view was mentioned by al-Imam as a possibility, and al-Qurtubi transmitted it, as Ibn Kathir said, from Muqatil; but it is among what is not relied upon. The sound and relied-upon view, as Ibn Hajar said in his commentary on al-Bukhari, is that it was revealed all at once from the Preserved Tablet to the House of Honour in the lowest heaven; indeed, some have related a consensus (ijma') on it. Yes, it is not far-fetched to say that the scribes (safara) there arranged it for Jibril (peace be upon him) on the nights mentioned.

Sayyid 'Isa al-Safawi answered that there is an objection to that, based on the permissibility of something like: "I speak, informing about speaking by your saying 'I speak'," and there is a difference of opinion on this between al-Dawani and others, which he mentioned in his treatise composed in answer to the question of al-Hadhar al-Asamm. Or it may be said: the pronoun returns to the Qur'an considered as a whole, setting aside its parts, so that the whole is spoken of with "We" (inna) revealed it, even though it is part of the whole: "Indeed We revealed it (inna anzalnahu)," which is included within its whole without any specific counterpart to it. They have mentioned that a part, insofar as it is independent, is different from it insofar as it is within the whole. In al-Itqan, from Abu Shama: If you say: "Indeed We revealed it," if it is not part of the Qur'an that was revealed all at once, then what was revealed all at once is not it; and if it is part of the whole, what is the meaning of this expression? I say: it has two aspects. One: the meaning is "Indeed We" decreed its revelation on the Night of Decree and determined it, and ordained it "and decreed it" in eternity. The second: the wording "anzalnahu" is in the past tense but its meaning is future; that is, its descent as a whole on the Night of Decree. End of quote. It has not become clear to me, in either of its two aspects, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, that there is any elegance, so consider this carefully, perhaps you will see.

It has been said: the meaning is: "Indeed We revealed it" concerning the excellence of the Night of Decree or concerning its status and worth; so the speech is according to an omitted noun (taqdir mudaf), or the adverbial sense of the place is metaphorical, as in the saying of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "I feared that a Qur'an would be revealed concerning me," and the saying of 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her): "Indeed I consider myself too lowly that a Qur'an should be revealed concerning me." Some made the "li" in that causal, and the pronoun refers to the Qur'an in the sense that revolves between the whole and the part. It has been said: it means the surah, and there is no objection to the fact that "Indeed We revealed it therein" for what has passed just now; so there is no need to say that what is meant by it is other than "Indeed We revealed it on the Night of Decree." It has been said: it is permissible that what is meant is the whole, since it includes that. In any case, interpreting the verse according to this meaning is not relied upon; what is relied upon is what has preceded. The meaning of revelation is the manifestation of the Qur'an from the world of the unseen to the world of witness, or establishing it with the scribes there, or something of this kind which does not make its attribution to the Qur'an problematic.

They differed concerning that night. It has been said that it is specified by a report about it, and that is, as al-Kirmani said, an error, because the end of the report refutes it, and the intended meaning is the lifting of its specification in it. It is related from 'Ikrima that it is the night of the middle of Sha'ban, and this is an anomalous, strange view, as in Tuhfat al-Muhtaj. The apparent sense here, together with the apparent sense of His saying, "The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed," refutes it. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that it moves through the nights of the year, so that in each year it falls on one night; al-Nawawi attributed this to Abu Hanifa and his two companions. But the majority hold that it is in the month of Ramadan. It is related from Ibn Razin that it is the first night of it. From al-Hasan al-Basri, the seventeenth, because the Battle of Badr took place on its morning; and it is also reported from Zayd ibn Arqam and Ibn Mas'ud.

And from Anas, as a marfu' report, the nineteenth.

It is also reported as a mawquf report from Ibn Mas'ud; and from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, the twenty-first, because of what is in the two Sahihs and others from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he (peace be upon him) said: "I saw this night, meaning the Night of Decree, and then I was made to forget it, and I saw myself prostrating on the morning of it in water and mud."

Abu Sa'id said: The sky rained that night, and the mosque leaked, and my eyes saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with traces of water and mud on his forehead and nose, from the morning of the twenty-first. In Muslim it is from the morning of the twenty-third. And from it, together with what precedes it, al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) inclined to the view that it is the twenty-first or the twenty-third night.

Ahmad, Muslim and others related from 'Abdullah ibn Unays that he was asked about the Night of Decree, and he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Seek it tonight,' and that night was the night of the twenty-third."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Jarir and others related from Bilal, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The Night of Decree is the night of the twenty-fourth.'" In al-Itqan and elsewhere it is said that it is the night in which the Qur'an was revealed.

Ibn Abi Shayba related from Abu Dharr that he was asked about the Night of Decree and said: "'Umar, Huthayfa and some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not doubt that it is the night of the twenty-seventh."

Ibn Nasr and Ibn Jarir in his Tahdhib related from Mu'awiya, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Seek the Night of Decree in the last night of Ramadan.'"

In the narration of Ahmad from Abu Hurayra, as a marfu' report, that it is the last night.

It has been said: it is in the middle ten, moving within it; it has been said: on its odd nights, and it has been said: on its even nights.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from 'A'isha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Seek the Night of Decree on the odd nights of the last ten nights of the month of Ramadan."

In a hadith related by Ahmad and a group from 'Ubada ibn al-Samit as a marfu' report, and two hadiths related by Ibn Jarir and others from Jabir ibn Samura, and from 'Abdullah ibn Jabir likewise, there is what indicates what has been mentioned as well. Indeed, the authentic reports indicating it are numerous. In sum, the views concerning it are very varied; but the majority hold that it is in the last ten nights, because of the many authentic hadiths on that, and most of them hold that it is on its odd nights for that reason too; and many of them held that it is the seventh night from those odd nights.

It is authentically transmitted from the narration of Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and others that Zirr ibn Hubaysh asked Ubayy ibn Ka'b about it, and he swore without making an exception that it is the night of the twenty-seventh. He (Zirr) said to him: "By what do you say that, O Abu al-Mundhir?"

He said: "By the sign which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned: that on its morning the sun rises without a ray of light."

Some reports from Ibn 'Abbas are apparent in this regard. And in some of the supporting evidence for it, there is what indicates the grandeur of the status of the number seven, which they said is a complete number: from the seven heavens, the seven earths, the seven days, the seven pebbles, the seven circuits around the House, prostration upon seven limbs, and other things mentioned, since you know of the authentic and mutually corroborating reports. It is a time of the weakness of the body, in which the reward of deeds increases, and a time of the strength of readiness for the manifestations (tajalliyat) for greater purification; and that it is on odd nights is more hopeful according to the hadiths as well, together with the fact that Allah, exalted is He, is Witr (One) and loves the odd.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami said: a group has chosen that it is not fixed to one specific night of the last ten, but moves through its nights: in one year, or several years, it falls on an odd night, one, three, or others; and in one year, or several years, on an even night, two, four, or others. They said: the conflicting hadiths about it cannot be reconciled except by this.

The words of al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) in reconciling the hadiths require it. End of quote. It is not hidden that reconciling conflicting hadiths about it in this way, in absolute terms, is not feasible; reconciliation in this way is feasible only with reference to the ten nights. It has been said, regarding reconciliation in general, that it moves, and that what is authentically established as a specification, in general or in verified form, is to be understood as referring to the Night of Decree in a particular month of Ramadan: that the Prophet (ﷺ) knew it was on the first night of a certain month of Ramadan, so he said: "It is the night of such-and-such."

That is, in this particular month of Ramadan. And he (ﷺ) knew that in the following Ramadan it was on another night, different from the one he mentioned earlier, so he said: "It is the night of such-and-such."

And he (ﷺ) knew that at its end, in the last ten of it, so he said: "It is in the last ten."

Meaning: from this particular month, and so on, and it is as you see. On the view that it moves between the nights, some have claimed that if the first night of the month falls on such-and-such, then it is the twenty-seventh night, and if the first night falls on such-and-such, then it is the twenty-first night, to the end of what he said. We have mentioned this together with its wording in *al-Tiraz al-Mudhahhab*, and there is nothing in it that constitutes a proof against others.

Some reports mention signs of it. In the hadith of Imam Ahmad, al-Bayhaqi and others, related from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, among its signs: it is a night of clear brightness, calm and serene, neither hot nor cold, as if there were a shining moon in it, and no star is shot down in it until morning.

Ibn Jarir, in his *Tahdhib*, and Ibn Mardawayh recorded something similar, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). If this is authentic, then to understand it as referring to the Night of Qadr in a specific Ramadan is practically required, since it is neither consistent nor predominant, as far as appears.

The wisdom in concealing it is that the one seeking it should strive in worship at other times, so that he may chance upon it, such as by spending all the nights of Ramadan in worship, as was the custom of the early generations (al-salaf). Al-Imam (al-Razi) has a statement on this matter which is too exalted to be spoken in such a manner; by my life, he erred here in a manifest slip, and said something that is close to indicating his ignorance.

The meaning of Laylat al-Qadr is the Night of Decree (taqdir), and it was so named because of what is related from Ibn Abbas and others: that in it is decreed and determined what will occur in that year of rain, provision, life and death, until the following year. The purpose is to make manifest His exalted decree of that to the angels (peace be upon them) who are charged with the worldly events. Otherwise, His exalted decree of all things is eternal, before the creation of the heavens and the earth. However, some of the eminent scholars said: the occurrence of the decree on this night is problematic, given the view of many that it is the night of the middle of Shaban, which is the intended "blessed night" in which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Therein is made distinct every wise matter﴾. He answered that there are three things here:

The first is the very decreeing of matters, meaning the determination of their measures and times, and that is in eternity. The second is the manifestation of those measures to the angels (peace be upon them) by their being written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz); and that is on the night of the middle of Shaban. The third is the establishment of those measures in copies, and their delivery to their custodians from among the "arrangers" (al-mudabbirat, the angels charged with administering affairs). So the copy of provisions, plants and rains is handed to Mika'il (peace be upon him); the copy of wars, winds, armies, earthquakes, thunderbolts and sinking of land to Jibril (peace be upon him); the copy of deeds to Israfil (peace be upon him); and the copy of calamities to the Angel of Death. And that is on the Night of Qadr. It was also said: on the night of the middle (of Shaban) the terms and provisions are decreed, and on the Night of Qadr the matters in which there is good, blessing and safety. It was also said: on this night is decreed what pertains to the honouring of the religion and what contains great benefit for the Muslims; and on the night of the middle (of Shaban) the names of those who will die are written and handed over to the Angel of Death. And Allah the Exalted knows best the reality of the matter.

Al-Zuhri said: the meaning is the Night of Greatness and Nobility, from their saying: "a man who has qadr with so-and-so," that is, a rank and honour. It was named so because whoever performs acts of obedience in it becomes one of qadr and honour with Allah, Mighty and Majestic; or because acts of obedience have that (qadr) in it. It was also said: because a book of great worth was revealed in it, through an angel of great worth, upon the Messenger of Allah, who is of great worth, for a community of great worth. And it was said: because angels of great worth descend in it. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: the meaning is the Night of Constriction, from "qudira alayhi rizquhu" (his provision was constricted), and it was named so because the earth becomes constricted in it by the angels (peace be upon them). Its being better than a thousand months, in terms of worship, according to the majority, means that worship in it is better than worship in a thousand months. The exact measure of its superiority is known only to Him, glory be to Him. This is a bounty from Him, Exalted, and He, Mighty and Majestic, may specify whomever He wills with whatever He wills, and a small deed may be better than a great deed.

This does not contradict the principle that whatever is more and more arduous is more excellent, because of the report in Muslim that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her): "Your reward is according to your toil."

[This is because it is a general tendency, as many have said. And there is no doubt that a small deed may surpass a great deed in terms of time, place, and manner of performance, such as one prayer performed in congregation, which equals twenty-five times a similar prayer performed alone, and so on. Yes, this excellence may be understood in some cases and not in others, as in what we are discussing; and there is no restriction upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and none knows what is with Him, glory be to Him, except Him, exalted is His state.]

As for the specification of the thousand by mention, it has been said that it is either for multiplicity, as in His saying: ﴿Each one of them wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾; and numbers are often intended in this sense. In al-Bahr there is a report that the meaning according to this is "better than the entire age." Or it is because of what Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan recorded from Mujahid: that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned a man from the Children of Israel who carried weapons in the cause of Allah for a thousand months, so the Muslims were amazed at that and their own deeds seemed meagre to them, so Allah revealed the surah.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ali ibn Urwah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned one day four men from the Children of Israel who worshipped Allah for eighty years without disobeying Him for the blink of an eye: Ayyub, Zakariyya, Hizqil ibn al-Ajuz, and Yusha ibn Nun. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were amazed at that. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said: "O Muhammad, your community is amazed at the worship of these men for eighty years, but Allah has sent down to you something better than that." Then he recited to him: ﴿Indeed, We revealed it﴾ to the end. Then he said: "This is better than what you and your community were amazed at." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased with that.

It was also said: in former times a man was not called "worshipper" until he had worshipped Allah for a thousand months; so they were given a night, which if they revived it, they would be more deserving of being called worshippers than those worshippers.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the reign of each of Sulayman and Dhu al-Qarnayn was five hundred months, so Allah made the deed on this night, for whoever attains it, better than their two reigns. In this there is consideration: if by Dhu al-Qarnayn is meant the first, then according to the view that he is him, he ruled much more than that by a great deal; and if by him is meant the second, namely the slayer of Dara, then he ruled much less than that by a great deal.

It was also said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was shown the lifespans of all the nations, and he considered the lifespans of his community short, and feared, may prayer and peace be upon him, that they would not reach the same amount of deed as others did in a long life. So Allah gave him the Night of Qadr and made it better than a thousand months for all the other nations. Imam Malik mentioned this in the Muwatta.

I have heard what indicates that the "thousand" is an allusion to the reign of the Banu Umayyah. According to what al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl said, it was a thousand months, neither one day more nor one day less; according to what has been said, eighty years, which is approximately a thousand months, since it is eighty-three years and four months. Their rule over the island of al-Andalus afterwards does not contradict this, because it was a small kingdom in some corners of the earth and at the far end of the inhabited lands of the Arabs; and for this reason, those of their caliphs who ruled there are not counted among their caliphs.

They also said that their (the Umayyads') extinction was with the death of Marwan al-Himar. Qadi Abd al-Jabbar objected to the verse being an allusion to what was mentioned, on the grounds that the days of the Banu Umayyah were blameworthy; that is, in the general sense. Therefore it would be remote to say concerning that night that it is better than a thousand blameworthy months:

*Do you not see that the sword loses its worth*
*when it is said that the sword is better than the staff?*

It was answered that those days were great according to worldly felicities, so it is not remote that Allah the Exalted says: "I have given you a night in religious felicities which is better than those in worldly felicities, so no benefit remains." 

It was disputed whether that night carries its day along with it or not. Al-Sha'bi said: yes, its day is like it. It was said: perhaps the reason for this is that mention of nights implies days, and from this: if one vows to observe seclusion (i'tikaf) for two nights, both nights and their two days become obligatory; but if he vows many nights, they do not. However, it has been said that it is recommended to strive in worship on its day as it is recommended on its night. For this reason, it is described that the sun rises on its morning without rays, as has been previously mentioned, that is, because of the greatness of the lights of the angels ascending and descending in it. For there is no benefit in it except knowing its day, and there is no benefit in it if striving in its day were not recommended.

This was objected to: it is possible that the benefit is knowing the night itself, so that one may strive in it in a subsequent year, based on the view that it does not move. The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is better than the Night of Friday, and the matter is one of difference of opinion. Most of the imams hold that it is better than it, because of the verse; and because Allah the Exalted sent down the Qur'an in it, and He did not send it down in any other night; and because He, glorified, commanded that it be sought. Ibn Abbas said concerning His saying: ﴿And seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾ that it refers to the Night of Qadr. And because He, Mighty and Majestic, made it the Night of Distinction and Judgment, and He, exalted is His majesty, said: ﴿Therein is made distinct every wise matter﴾, and He named it, exalted and high, the Night of Qadr, that is, of Decree. And because of what is related from Ka'b, who said: Allah the Exalted chose the hours, and He chose the hours of the times of prayer; and He chose the days, and He chose Friday; and He chose the months, and He chose the month of Ramadan; and He chose the nights, and He chose the Night of Qadr. So it is the best night in the best month. And because the Prophet (ﷺ) urged deeds in it; for it is authentic: "Whoever stands in worship on the Night of Qadr out of faith and seeking reward, his previous sins will be forgiven." And in another narration: "and what was delayed."

The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade that the Night of Friday be singled out for night prayer and its day for fasting. And because He, glorified and exalted, concealed it and did not specify it, just as He concealed His greatest Name, Mighty and Majestic, and just as He, exalted is His majesty, concealed the best of prayers, which is the Middle Prayer (al-Salat al-Wusta), and so on.

Most of the Hanbalis, such as Abu al-Hasan al-Jazari, Abd Allah ibn Battah, Abu Hafs al-Barmaki and others, held that the Night of Friday is better, because of what Muqatil recorded from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah forgives the Night of Friday for all the people of Islam, and this is a virtue not found in any other."

Similar to this is what is related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no Friday night but that Allah looks upon His creation three times, and forgives whoever does not associate anything with Allah."

Because Ibn Bashkuwal recorded in his book, *al-Qurbah ila Rabb al-Alamin*, with his chain traced to Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Increase your prayers upon me on the radiant night and the bright day: the Night of Friday and the Day of Friday."

Al-Ghurrah from something is its best. Also, many have narrated, including Imam Ahmad, that its day is the lord of days and the greatest of them, and greater with Allah, Exalted, than the Day of Fitr and the Day of Adha.

Ibn Hibban authenticated the report: "The sun does not rise nor set upon a day better than the Day of Friday."

Therefore it is the lady of nights, the greatest and the best of them. And because it is specified and witnessed, which the elite and the common, male and female, young and old, seeing and blind, witness; and its blessing reaches the living and the dead. Whereas the Night of Qadr is not specified, so only a few benefit from it, and so on.

Those who held this view answered the verse by saying that when it is taken to mean that it is better than a thousand months in which there is no Laylat al-Qadr, as Qatadah and others said, then it should equally be taken to mean that it is better than a thousand months in which there is no Friday night (laylat al-jumu'ah). Both points are supported by the fact that most of the earlier occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) indicate that the "months" meant are the months of earlier nations, and those months contained neither Laylat al-Qadr nor a Friday night. As for the other evidences (al-mustanadat), some of them conflict with one another, and others only indicate its excellence, which no one denies. The earlier scholars answered their own evidences in a similar way to how the others answered. Because of this conflict, Ahmad ibn al-Husayn ibn Ya'qub ibn Qasim al-Muqri, a Hanbali (a follower of the Hanbali school), said: "The two opinions on this question are both widely held among the scholars, and each has evidence that supports its correctness. So no one should describe the proponent of either one as being in error." After you reflect on the evidences of both sides and understand their circumstances, the superiority of Laylat al-Qadr and the particular virtue of Friday night will become clear to you. There is also an intermediate opinion between the two views. Qadi Abu Ya'la reported that Abu al-Hasan al-Tamimi, also a Hanbali, used to say: "The Night of Power in which the Qur'an was revealed is better than Friday night, because of the great good that occurred in it and did not occur in any other night. But as for the other nights of power, Friday night is better than them." It has also been said that the parallel to this is the Night of the Ascension (Laylat al-Mi'raj) compared with Friday night and similar nights.

Furthermore, the apparent meaning of the words of some Hanafis, such as the author of al-Jawharah, is that the Night of Sacrifice (Laylat al-Nahr) is better than Laylat al-Qadr and all other nights of the year. The apparent meaning of the verse also presents a problem for this view, and he would probably answer it in a similar way to what was mentioned just above.

Al-Tahawi, may God have mercy on him, reported in the margins of al-Mukhtar (Hawashi al-Mukhtar) from some Shafi'is (followers of the Shafi'i school) that the most excellent nights are the Night of the Prophet's Birth (ﷺ), then Laylat al-Qadr, then the Night of the Isra' and Mi'raj, then the Night of 'Arafah, then Friday night, then the middle night of Sha'ban, then the Night of 'Eid. I do not see that he has any basis to rely upon for this.

And God knows best.

What has been pointed out, that this night is one of the special features of this Ummah, is what most of the reports about the occasion of revelation indicate, and al-Haytami and others stated it explicitly. Al-Qastallani said: "It is objected to by the hadith of Abu Dharr in al-Nasa'i, where he said: 'O Messenger of God, will it continue to exist alongside the prophets, and when they die will it be lifted?' He (ﷺ) said: 'No, rather it continues to exist.'"

He then mentioned that the principal basis for those who hold this view is the report we presented earlier in the occasion of revelation, concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) seeing how short the lifespans of his Ummah were compared with the lifespans of earlier nations. He then followed this with the statement: "This is open to interpretation, so it does not override the explicit wording in the hadith of Abu Dharr, as the two hadith masters Ibn Kathir in his tafsir and Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari have said." (end of quotation). The correct view is the first one, and the explicit statement is beyond dispute.

Al-Daylami reported from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "God Almighty has granted my Ummah the Night of Power, which He did not give to those who came before them." So reflect on this and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 97, verse 4:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the basis of its excellence over that long span of time. The pronoun in "therein" (fiha) refers to the night. Some scholars claimed that the clause is a description (sifah) of "a thousand months," with the pronoun referring to it, but this is not correct. Some also permitted that the pronoun refers to the angels, with "the Spirit" being a subject (mubtada') rather than conjoined to "the angels," and "therein" being its predicate rather than being connected to "descend," and the clause being a circumstantial phrase (hal) of "the angels." But this contradicts the apparent meaning.

According to the majority, "the Spirit" is Jibril (peace be upon him). He was singled out for mention to show his high rank, even though he is the one who descends with the Reminder. It was also said that he is a great angel who, if he were to swallow the heavens and the earth, they would be a single morsel for him. The Tafsir (al-Taysir) mentions descriptions of him that overwhelm the intellects, and Allah Most High knows best the soundness of the report.

Ka'b and Muqatil said: "The Spirit is a group of angels whom the (other) angels do not see except on that night, like the ascetics whom we do not see except on the day of 'Id or Friday." It was said: they are guardians over the angels, like the guarding angels over us. It was said: they are a creation of Allah Most High who eat and dress, who are neither angels nor humans, and ﴿He creates what you do not know﴾, and ﴿None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾. According to what has been said, they may be the servants of the people of Paradise. It was also said: it is Jesus (peace be upon him), who descends to look after this community and to visit the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: they are the spirits of believers who descend to visit their families. It was said: it is mercy, as was read: ﴿Do not despair of the mercy (rawh) of Allah﴾ with a damma. But the first view is the one relied upon. The apparent meaning, which the reports support, is that the descent is to the earth. It was said: this is because of what Allah Most High mentions afterward, and its discussion will come, if Allah Most High wills. It was said: they descend to it in order to greet the believers. It was said: because Allah Most High made the virtue of this night lie in devoting oneself to His worship on earth, so they descend to it so that their acts of worship may be greater in reward, just as a man among us goes to Makkah so that his worship will be (greater) in the same way. The purpose of informing of this is to encourage a person to obey.

Isam al-Din said: It is possible that their descent is for the purpose of catching up with it, since there is no night in the heaven, and in that case the clause confirms what came before rather than explaining the basis of the excellence. But this has a problem that is not hidden.

Other views have been stated besides these, which we will point out, if Allah Most High wills. It was said: the intended meaning is their descent to the lowest heaven, which is contrary to what comes to mind first. Much further from this is the view that the intended meaning of their descent is their descent from their lofty ranks of occupation with Allah Most High and absorption in contemplating His majesty, in order to greet the believers.

It has been argued that the intended meaning of "the angels" (peace be upon them) is all of them. But this raises the difficulty that they are in very great number, which neither the earth nor the lowest heaven can hold, since the lowest heaven is full before their descent. (The Prophet (ﷺ) said): "The heaven has groaned, and it has the right to groan. There is not a place the width of a foot in it without an angel who is prostrating, bowing, or standing." This was answered by saying that they descend in groups, group after group, so some are descending and some ascending, like pilgrims who, despite their numbers, enter the Ka'bah all together, for example, but not in a manner of gathering together; rather, some are entering and some leaving. The use of "descend" (tanazzalu), which indicates gradualness, rather than "descended" (nazala), is a hint to this. It was also said: since they are lights, there is no crowding among them. A light that fills a room, for example, does not prevent a thousand other lights from entering upon it. But as you see, this is weak.

Some people restricted the angels to certain of their categories, namely the inhabitants of the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), or some of them.

In al-Ghunyah by the Rabbani Pole, Shaykh Abd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may Allah sanctify his secret, it is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When it is the Night of Power, Allah Most High commands Jibril (peace be upon him) to descend to the earth, and with him are the inhabitants of the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, seventy thousand angels, and with them are banners of light. When they descend to the earth, Jibril (peace be upon him) plants his banner, and the angels (peace be upon them) plant their banners at four places: near the Ka'bah, the grave of the Prophet (ﷺ), the Masjid of Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Masjid of Mount Sinai. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) says: 'Disperse!' So they disperse, and no house, no stone, no dwelling, and no ship in which there is a believing man or woman remains but that the angels (peace be upon them) enter it, except a house in which there is a dog, a pig, wine, a person in a state of major impurity from what is unlawful, or images. They glorify, sanctify, declare Allah's oneness, and seek forgiveness for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the time of dawn. Then they ascend to the heaven, and the inhabitants of the lowest heaven receive them and say to them: 'From where have you come?' They say: 'We were in the world, because tonight is the Night of Power for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).' The inhabitants of the lowest heaven say: 'What has Allah Most High done with the needs of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ)?' Jibril (peace be upon him) says: 'Allah Most High has forgiven its righteous and interceded for its wicked.' Then the angels of the lowest heaven raise their voices in glorification, sanctification, and praise of the Lord of the worlds, thanking Him for what Allah Most High has given this community of forgiveness and good pleasure. Then the angels of the lowest heaven escort them to the second, and so on, likewise, up to the seventh. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) says: 'O inhabitants of the heavens, return!' So the angels of each heaven return to their places. When they reach the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, its inhabitants say to them: 'Where were you?' They answer them as they answered the inhabitants of the heavens. The inhabitants of the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary raise their voices in glorification, declaring Allah's oneness, and praise, and the Garden of Refuge hears, then the Garden of Bliss, the Garden of Eden, and the Firdaws hear, and the Throne of the Most Merciful hears, and the Throne raises its voice in glorification, declaring Allah's oneness, and praise of the Lord of the worlds, thanking Him for what He has given this community. It says: 'My God, it has reached me from You that You forgave last night the righteous of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) and interceded for its righteous.' Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: 'You have spoken truly, O My Throne. For the community of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), with Me is honor that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human being.'"

In another report from Ka'b: all the angels of the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary descend together with Jibril (peace be upon them), and none knows their number except Allah Most High, and Jibril (peace be upon him) does not leave anyone among the people without shaking his hand.

In another report: he does not leave a believing man or believing woman without greeting them, except the habitual drinker of wine, the eater of pork, and the one who smears himself with saffron. The sign of his shaking hands (peace be upon him) is the rising of the skin, the softening of the heart, and the tears of the eyes.

Other accounts have been transmitted about his descent with the angels (peace be upon them) and his ascent with them, and the Imam and others have mentioned some of these. We ask Allah Most High for the soundness of the reports.

Some have mentioned that on that night Jibril (peace be upon him) distributes what descends of the mercy of Allah Most High, which covers the living believers. He says: "My Lord, much of the mercy remains. What shall I do with it?" Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: "Distribute it among the dead of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ)." He distributes it until it covers them. Then he says: "My Lord, much of the mercy remains. What shall I do with it?" The Glorified and Exalted says: "Distribute it among the disbelievers." He distributes it among them, and whoever among them receives some of that mercy dies upon faith.

﴿By the permission of their Lord﴾ is connected to "descend," or to a deleted element that is a circumstantial phrase (hal) of its subject; that is, "while being accompanied by the permission of their Lord," meaning by His command, Mighty and Majestic. Restricting it with this is to magnify the matter of their descent. It was also said: the indication is that they desire the believers on earth and long for them, so they seek permission and are granted it. There is in this a kind of encouragement to strive in obedience. The question was raised about this desire given the abundance of sins, and it was answered that they are not aware of its details, or they did not consider them as preventing that, because they see among the kinds of obedience what they do not see in the heaven, or in order to hear the groaning of the sinners who repent.

So in the sacred hadith: "The groaning of the sinners is more beloved to Me than the chanting of those who glorify."

Or in order to meet with those who have a connection with them among the truthful (siddiqun), to perform the customs of love. For the spirits of the truthful, stripped of the garments of the bodies, have continued to visit the angels (peace be upon them) in their places by ascending to them. So it is fitting that the angels (peace be upon them) visit them in their corners. Even if that requires gathering with others who are not like them, that is a secondary matter.

For the sake of one eye, a thousand eyes are honored.

﴿For every matter﴾: that is, for the sake of every matter connected to the decree for that year until the next, which Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, showed them. So said more than one scholar, and "min" (from) has the meaning of the causal "li" (for), connected to "descend." Isam al-Din said: If you ask: decrees are not carried out on that night, but in the course of the year. Why then do the angels (peace be upon them) descend in it for the sake of those matters? I say: perhaps their descent is to determine the execution of those matters for them, and their descending for the sake of every matter is not in the sense that each one descends for the sake of each matter, nor that each one descends for a matter, but in the sense that all of them descend for the sake of all the matters, so that in the speech there is a division of causes among the effects. End.

I say: it is possible that their descent is to prepare the receptacles to accept what they have been commanded, and by what he mentioned of the division, he pointed out that it is permissible for one of them to descend for several matters. As for their saying "for the sake of every matter, connected to..." etc., what it contains of discussion has already been mentioned, so consider it.

Abu Hatim said: "min" has the meaning of "bi" (with), that is, they descend with every matter. It was said: that is, of good and blessing. It was said: of good and evil. On this view, "ba'" is causal, and the meaning returns to something like what has passed. Some made it indicate accompaniment, and the intended meaning of their accompaniment of it is their being charged with the command concerning it, as if it were said: the angels descend while they are commanded with every matter that occurs in the year. Their descending while being in that state does not require their doing all that they were commanded in that night. The apparent meaning, according to what they said, is that the intended meaning of "the angels" is the ones who manage affairs (al-mudabbirat), since others have no connection to the matters for which the decree is made, so that they would descend for their sake, in the earlier sense. This contradicts what the reports indicate of their not being restricted to those who manage affairs, so reflect. And perhaps for this reason it was said that ﴿for every matter﴾ is connected to the saying of Him, Exalted is He:

[Page 197 continues]

﴿Peace﴾: it is a verbal noun meaning safety (*salamah*), and it is the predicate placed before its subject (*khabar muqaddam*). The phrase ﴿it﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*). The meaning is: it is peace from every frightening matter. Its connection to *bi-dhalika* (with that) is by way of extension in the adverbial phrase; otherwise, according to the well-known view, the complement of a verbal noun may not precede it. It has also been said that it is connected to an elided word placed before it, which the mentioned word explains. Whoever has read the words of al-'Allamah al-Taftazani (d. 792 AH) at the beginning of his commentary on *al-Talkhis* regarding such a case will not need what has been mentioned. It has also been said that ﴿from every matter﴾ is connected to *tanazzalu* (they descend), but with the sense that they descend to the earth separated from every matter that is theirs in the heavens and leaving it. In this there is an indication of the great concern with the descent to the earth. In it there is also a degree of remoteness.

The fronting of the predicate serves restriction, as in the saying: "I am Tamimi" (meaning, I am only a Tamimi). The predication with the verbal noun is for emphasis; that is, it is nothing but completely safe, to the point that it is as if it were the very essence of safety. Al-Dahhak said regarding this meaning: "Indeed He, exalted is He, does not decree or judge in it except safety." It was said: that is, His decree does not take effect and His judgment is not tied to anything except that. Its summary is that nothing exists except that. Mujahid said: "It is safe from Satan and his harm." It is related that Satan does not come out on the Night of Decree until its dawn appears, and he is unable to afflict anyone in it with madness, disease, or any kind of corruption, and no sorcerer's magic takes effect in it. Perhaps what occurs of sins on this night comes from the commanding self (*al-nafs al-ammarah*) and not through the mediation of Satan. The statement of al-Dahhak was found problematic, based on what was said about it: that no night is free of evil and frightening matters, and there is no originator except Allah, mighty and majestic. So perhaps he meant what was previously transmitted, not far from this: that Allah, exalted is He, only decrees safety and goodness in this night; that is, He does not manifest to the angels, peace be upon them, except His decree, mighty and majestic. It was also said: "It is nothing but peace," in the manner of: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, is nothing but mercy." The meaning is that it is a complete cause of safety and deliverance from destructions on the Day of Resurrection, since whoever stands in it in faith and seeking reward, his previous sins are forgiven. It was said: *al-salam* is a verbal noun meaning greeting (*al-taslim*); that is, it is nothing but greeting, because of the abundance of greeting and of those greeting, from the angels, upon the believers in it. This was related from al-Sha'bi and Mansur, and they made it the very essence of greeting for emphasis as well.

The words of the Exalted ﴿until the emergence of dawn﴾ are a limit (*ghayah*) showing the generality of safety or greeting throughout the whole night. The preposition is connected to *salam* (peace), and *matla'* is a noun of time. They have stated explicitly that it is from *yaf'ulu* (to rise), and *yaf'ulu*, with the 'ayn vowelled either fatha or damma, is on the pattern *maf'il*, with the 'ayn fathah. It is also permitted that it be a mimi verbal noun meaning rising, and this requires an elided genitive word before it, such as "time" or what is in its meaning, so that the limit and the limited are of one kind. The connection of the preposition to this is valid despite the separation, because it is not a verbal noun, considering the reality. Al-Tabarsi and others stated that it must be interpreted as *salimah* (safe) or *musallamah* (greeted) in order for the connection to be valid. But if it is kept in its verbal-noun status, it is not valid, because of the necessary separation between the relative clause and the relative pronoun. Some scholars held that the separation between the verbal noun and its complement by the subject is excusable. It was also permitted that the limit be connected to *tanazzalu* (they descend), in the sense that their descent does not cease, group after group, until the time of the emergence of dawn. This was criticised as far-fetched, because *salam* is then a foreign element, and it is not a parenthetical interjection, so separation by it is not good; nor is making it a circumstantial (*hal*) of the pronoun in the genitive in His words ﴿in it﴾, that is, possessing safety or peace, whose condition is not hidden. It was said: it is permitted that the pause be on *salam*, and it is the predicate of an elided subject, and ﴿from every matter﴾ is connected to it, and ﴿it﴾ is a subject, and ﴿until the emergence of dawn﴾ is its predicate.

Al-Tibi, al-Tabarsi, and others did not permit this, saying: because there is no benefit in predicating of it that it is until the emergence of dawn, since every night is like this. It was answered: when He informed about it that it is better than a thousand months, and it was understood that it differs from the other nights in quality, and this was a basis for suspecting that its very essence in measure also differs from the essences of the other nights, this suspicion was removed by His saying: "it is until the emergence of dawn," that is, it did not differ from the other nights in that, even though it differed in excellence and goodness.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, and al-Kalbi read: "from every *imri'*" with a hamza at its end; that is, they descend for the sake of every person, that is, for the sake of what concerns him of what is decreed in that night, which returns to what was previously mentioned, or for the sake of his welfare, such as seeking forgiveness for him and the like, on the basis that what is meant by this is every believing man, as was said. It was said: the preposition is connected to *salam*, and what is meant by "every *imri'*" is the angels, peace be upon them; that is, it is peace and greeting upon the believers from every angel. Abu Hatim, as Ibn Jinni said, denied this reading. Abu Raja', al-A'mash, Ibn Thabit, Talhah, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Kisa'i, and Abu 'Amr (with a variant from him) read: "*matli'*" (with a kasra on the lam), as a verbal noun on the pattern of *al-marji'* (the return), and an elided genitive word is assumed, as you have heard, or it is a noun of time by unanalogical usage, like *al-mashriq* (the place of sunrise), since *maf'il* with a kasra is the analogical form of *yaf'ilu* with a kasra on the 'ayn. In *al-Bahr* it is said: "*matla'* and *matli'*," with fatha and kasra, are both verbal nouns in the dialect of Tamim. It was also said: the verbal noun is with fatha, and the place of rising with kasra, according to the people of the Hijaz, end of quotation. Taking it to mean a place here has no place, as is not hidden. Know that it is recommended to supplicate on this blessed night, and it is one of the times when supplications are answered.

Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and others transmitted from 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, if I happen upon the Night of Decree, what should I say?" He said: "Say: O Allah, You are Forgiving, You love forgiveness, so forgive me."

One should exert oneself in it with various kinds of worship, such as prayer and other acts. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Supplication on that night is better than prayer." Then he stated that if one recites and supplicates, it is good. The Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to exert himself in the nights of the month of Ramadan, and he would recite in them slowly and measuredly; he would not pass a verse of mercy without asking, nor a verse of punishment without seeking refuge. Ibn Rajab mentioned that the most perfect is to combine prayer, recitation, supplication, and reflection. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to do all of that, especially in the last ten nights, and its standing (*qiyam*) is realised, according to what some said, by the Tarawih prayer.

al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "Whoever prays the Maghrib and the 'Isha' in congregation until the month of Ramadan ends, has obtained a full share of the Night of Decree."

Malik, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Zanjawayh, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "Whoever attends the 'Isha' prayer on the Night of Decree in congregation has taken his share of it."

In *Tuhfat al-Muhtaj* by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, may mercy be upon him, it is said: It is recommended for one who sees it to conceal it, and one does not attain its excellence, that is, its perfection, except one whom Allah, exalted is He, has made aware of it. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that by seeing it he meant perceiving by which knowledge of it is attained, from what it is distinguished by of lights and the descent of the angels, peace be upon them, or something similar to unveiling that yields knowledge, of a kind whose reality only its people know. This is nearly explicit that whoever Allah wills of His servants sees it. Abu Hafs ibn Shahin said, as Ibn Rajab related: Allah, exalted is He, did not unveil it to anyone of the earlier or later generations, nor to any of the prophets and messengers, on any day or night, except our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. For when He revealed it to him and made him aware of its status, He showed it to him, peace and blessings be upon him, in his dream, and informed him on which night it would be. So he awoke knowing it, and he wished to inform the people of it out of joy. Then two men quarrelled in his presence, and he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was caused to forget it, and he was commanded to seek it in the last ten nights, because they do not see it by unveiling ever, and no one sees it after him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, at all. So they were commanded to that, so that its excellence would be sought in the nights called (by that name). End of quotation.

The hadith that the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, saw it and forgot it has been transmitted by Imam Malik, Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others, and there is no doubt about its authenticity. But regarding its indication that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was not informed of it, did not see it afterward, and that none of his community sees it ever, there is hesitation. Perhaps the command to seek it in the last ten nights, for example, points to hope of seeing it in them, since what is not hoped for in a time or place is not good for anyone to be commanded to seek in it ordinarily. Some reports indicate that seeing it in a dream happened to others besides him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. In Sahih Muslim and others, from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, it is related that: "Some men among the companions of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, were shown the Night of Decree in a dream in the last seven nights. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, said: 'I see that your dreams have agreed on the last seven nights; so whoever seeks it, let him seek it in the last seven nights.'"

Something like the statement of Ibn Shahin has been related from others as well, and it was an error. In the *Sharh Sahih Muslim* of al-Nawawi: Know that the Night of Decree exists, that it is seen, and that whom Allah wills of the children of Adam realises it every year in Ramadan, as the hadiths and reports of the righteous have abundantly attested to it, and their sightings of it are more than can be counted. As for the statement of Qadi 'Iyad, transmitted from al-Muhallab ibn Abi Sufrah: "It is not possible to see it in reality," it is a gross error, and I have pointed it out lest one be deceived by it. End of quotation.

[Page 199]

There remains in the discussion of this night an important investigation: that according to the view of the authorities on the differences of the horizons (*ikhtilaf al-matali'*), it necessarily follows that it occurs more than once in Ramadan, and that it is an odd night of its nights according to some and an even night according to others. So it is not valid to state flatly that it is one of them, and likewise it is not valid to state flatly that it is the night of such-and-such, like the night of the twenty-seventh or the twenty-first of the month, for example, on that basis as well.

Rather, it is not valid to state absolutely that the time of the decree and the descent of the angels is a night, for night among one people is day in the region facing their feet, and that region may be inhabited, even if by means of a ship passing through it. Perhaps the time of night for some people is partly night and partly day for others, as with the inhabitants of some latitudes far from the equator. Indeed, months may pass with a night and a day for some people while not a single day has passed in some latitudes. Moreover, it is also not valid to state absolutely that it falls in Ramadan and that it is the first or last night of it, since the month's beginning and end differ with regard to the inhabitants of the earth.

Some have answered by accepting that what is stated about it is not absolute, so that it is odd in relation to some people and even in relation to others. Likewise the statement that it is such-and-such a night of the month, and by accepting that it is a night for some people while it is day for others. The expression "night" is used to take into account the place of the one upon whom the Qur'an was revealed, peace be upon him, and most of the believers in him, as if the region in line with their feet, where its night is day, has not been settled by Muslims; indeed, it is barely settled by them until Allah, exalted is He, inherits the earth and whoever is upon it.

He said: Wherever it is day for some people, it is not unlikely that Allah, exalted is He, gives its reward to whoever among others strives in the night of that day, and that He, glory be to Him, also gives that to whoever among them strives at night while it is day for them. The same applies to the cases mentioned in the discussion.

He claimed that this is a kind of reconciliation between conflicting hadiths, and that their saying "it is recommended to strive on its day" is a symbol for something of that sort. It is as you see. Another answered with something the pen is ashamed to mention, and considers leaving it aside to be most fitting for its rank.

I heard from some of my beloved friends that Shaykh Isma'il al-'Ajluni, may Allah have mercy on him, touched upon some of this discussion and its answer in what he explained of Sahih al-Bukhari, but I have not come across it. In my view the discussion is strong, and the matter is one in which my intellect has no room. Like the Night of Power, in what has been mentioned, is the time of His descent, glory be to Him and exalted, to the lowest heaven during the night, as authentic reports have confirmed; and likewise the hour of answered prayer on Friday, and other similar examples. Shaykh Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, has a lengthy discourse on the first, which I do not have at hand now to satisfy the thirst; and others, such as Ibn Hajar, have a brief discourse on the second, which is well known. It may perhaps be said that for every people, their night is their night, even though its beginning and end differ with regard to their horizons, just as with all their nights. So the night enters absolutely in Baghdad, for example, at sunset there, and after half an hour it enters Istanbul, for example; that is the first time of sunset there, and so on. Departure is the reverse of this. So the night is like a rider travelling in one direction, reaching every station at a time. It is required that the angels descend in accordance with its course. It is not unlikely that at each people's [region], at the first entry of the night among them, whomever Allah, exalted is He, wills of them descend, and they ascend at the break of its dawn among them as well; or the one who descends among them remains there until the night ends across the whole inhabited world, and then they ascend together when it ends. The view of multiplicity of decree according to its course is also maintained: Allah, exalted is He, decrees, in whatever part of it He wills, matters concerning those for whom it is night. The excellence for each people lies in the realisation of these matters in relation to them and their standing in them. Similar to this night, in what has been mentioned, are all the times of worship, such as the time of Dhuhr, 'Asr and others. This is the utmost that comes to mind regarding this problem. As for what disturbs it from solitary reports, it is easy, especially since many of them are open to question regarding their authenticity. So reflect on this, and may Allah, Mighty and Majestic, guide you.

Furthermore, the Night of Power, according to the Sufi masters, is a night in which the seeker is singled out with a special manifestation through which he recognises his station and rank in relation to his Beloved. It is the time when the seeker begins to arrive at the Essence of Unity (ʿayn al-jamʿ) and the station of those who have attained knowledge. How subtle is the saying of Shaykh 'Umar ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified:

"Every night becomes the Night of Power when it draws near, just as every day of union is a Friday."

This, and Allah the Exalted is the Guide to the straight path.
